topics.topic: Required Linux sandbox facility checks and startup refusal
questions: Must the mandatory sandbox probe still test the effective availability of namespaces and limits, or does the new no-host-testing rule remove or narrow that startup check?

On Linux lacking namespaces, limits, or another facility used by the sandbox, must the required sandbox probe produce the defined startup refusal, or is behavior wholly undefined because that host is unsupported?

quotes: probe_sandbox: [VALIDATION_ERROR] MUST raise SandboxUnavailableError naming what is missing when the bubblewrap executable, bwrap, cannot be found on the process's PATH, when bwrap --version, which prints "bubblewrap" and the version, names a version other than the imported RELEASE_BWRAP_VERSION constant, when the resolved interpreter path os.path.realpath(sys.executable) lies under no path of the imported SANDBOX_RUNTIME_PATHS constant, when that interpreter, the one execute_function starts inside bubblewrap, run once through bwrap with the same read-only bindings of the imported SANDBOX_RUNTIME_PATHS constant and the same links of the imported SANDBOX_ROOT_SYMLINKS constant to print platform.python_implementation() and platform.python_version() joined by one space, does not print exactly the imported RELEASE_SANDBOX_INTERPRETER constant, or when one probe execution through execute_function of a minimal implementation with no ports, under bounds equal to the imported RELEASE_CEILING_WALL_TIME_MS, RELEASE_CEILING_MEMORY_BYTES, RELEASE_CEILING_OUTPUT_BYTES and RELEASE_CEILING_PROCESS_COUNT constants, does not end succeeded, naming its outcome.

probe_sandbox: [RETURN_SHAPE] Returns None only when every check of its validation note holds — bwrap found, its version and the sandbox interpreter equal to the release's, and the probe execution succeeded; it writes no record.
judgement.why: State 6 explicitly preserves a probe using the real sandbox and release bounds and requires startup failure when that probe does not succeed.

topics.topic: SQLite database and journal path anchoring
questions: What pathname or directory-anchoring mechanism must the store give SQLite for the database and its later journal files: the original configured data-directory path, a path through the held directory descriptor, or another fixed mechanism?
Does SQLite open the database through a path anchored to the held data-directory descriptor, or through the original data-directory pathname?

quotes: Every file the store opens itself is opened relative to the data directory it holds open from the start, each component with Linux's `O_NOFOLLOW`, never first asking whether the flag exists (A20 rule 3); a link met so later makes that store call fail, writing no record (rule 3). The database file and its journal are opened by SQLite, which Python cannot ask to refuse a link — the journal being every file SQLite itself creates beside the database under the database's name, in whatever journal mode the database file holds; the kernel sets none and checks none; the start's check covers them, and the kernel does not watch them after it: in a private directory only the kernel's user or root can place a link, and either can change any record directly, so a link gives them nothing more (owner, 2026-10-18).

The database file and every file sqlite3 creates beside it under its name, in whatever journal mode the file holds, the module setting none, which sqlite3 opens and cannot be told to refuse a link, are checked only by open_store before the connection opens and are not watched after it (A18).

open_store: [BEHAVIOR] MUST run, in this order, stopping at the first failure: take an exclusive non-blocking lock on data_directory itself, reached component by component with os.O_NOFOLLOW (os.O_PATH for each directory on the way), opened for reading as a directory at its last component and held for the life of the process, so the lock creates no file; check that data_directory and everything inside it are owned by the process's effective user and grant no permission to group or others; walk the directory without following links and find no symbolic link; then open the database file inside data_directory as the module's one SQLite connection with synchronous FULL, after os.lstat finds that path no symbolic link; create its tables with create_store_schema, which leaves existing tables as they are; then remove the module's own temporary files left by an interrupted publish and every file of the content-addressed area whose digest no StoredValue names — a trial case's file fixture is itself a StoredValue of file carriage (M21), so no other record names a value file —, which is a digest for which list_stored_value_rows_by_value_digest answers no row, and create the content-addressed area and the spool area when absent.
judgement.divergence: One implementation gives SQLite a path anchored through the held data-directory descriptor, while another gives it the original configured pathname; after that pathname is renamed or replaced, SQLite can access different database or journal locations, which the owner and the store observe through different records, files, or failures.
judgement.why: Neither State 5 nor the later contracts specify how SQLite's pathname is anchored despite requiring the store to hold a directory descriptor.
judgement.deferred_to: the states whose texts it quotes

topics.topic: Whether configuration and credential files must be outside the data directory
questions: Is being outside the data directory an enforced installation constraint, or only explanatory threat-model text?
Must startup reject a configuration file or credential secret file located inside the kernel data directory, or is the statement that these paths lie outside it only non-normative rationale?

quotes: These paths lie outside the kernel's private directory, where another user may be able to place a link; that is what this rule guards (owner, 2026-10-18).

The installation's configuration file holds the owner token; the agent tokens; the selected manifest instance name of each service it selects one for; at most one credential for each service it gives one: a header name — an HTTP field-name token, or the kernel refuses to start — and the reference that resolves to its value on the host: the absolute path of a secret file, or the kernel refuses to start (a service with none fails only its own requests, rule 2); and the address the kernel's one `mcp` entrance listens on, which the host's reverse proxy reaches (owner, 2026-10-03, raised by the pre-contract data closure).

Checks in this order, the first failing one named: a regular private file of the kernel's user, not a link; one JSON object with exactly the installation's fields; no service twice among the selected instances or among the credentials; every credential header name an HTTP field-name token; every secret file reference an absolute path; tokens of at least 43 characters; tokens pairwise distinct; agent names pairwise distinct (A16 rule 1, A17 rule 1, M28).

A service credential is a header name and `secret_file`, the absolute path of a regular private file of the kernel's user whose content, without one trailing newline, is the value (A17 rules 1–2); the kernel reads no environment variable.
judgement.divergence: One implementation rejects at startup any configuration or secret path inside `data_directory`, while another accepts such private regular files and applies only the listed path and permission checks; the installer notices whether the kernel starts and whether the credential can be used.
judgement.why: The texts assert that the paths lie outside the private directory but never say whether that relationship is an enforced check or an assumed installation fact.

topics.topic: Configuration path reopening and anchoring during token refresh
questions: Does A16’s per-request change check reopen and resolve the configuration path component by component each time, or keep using a descriptor opened at startup (and therefore ignore pathname or ancestor replacement)?
